Content:
Given an I.I.D random sample from a probability distribution, suppose we needed to know the probability that the third largest value was less than [MATH: 10,] or the probability that the second smallest value was greater than [MATH: 5.]

Content:
To find such probabilities, we first need to put the values in the sample in ascending order. This is where we use so-called order statistics.

Content:
For an I.I.D random sample [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots X_n,] the order statistics are obtained by arranging the values in ascending order. The [MATH: r]th order statistic, denoted [MATH: X_{(r)},] is the [MATH: r]th smallest value in the ordered sample. Specifically,

Content:
- the first order statistic is [MATH: X_{(1)} = \min\left\{X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots, X_n\right\},]
- the second order statistic is [MATH: X_{(2)} =] the second smallest of [MATH: \left\{X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots, X_n\right\},]
- the third order statistic: [MATH: X_{(3)} =] the third smallest of [MATH: \left\{X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots, X_n\right\},]
- [MATH: \vdots]
- the [MATH: r]th order statistic is [MATH: X_{(r)} =] the [MATH: r]th smallest of [MATH: \left\{X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots, X_n\right\},]
- [MATH: \vdots]
- the [MATH: n]th order statistic is [MATH: X_{(n)} = \max\left\{X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots, X_n\right\}.]

Content:
To demonstrate, consider the following sample taken from the I.I.D random sample [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_5.]

Content:
[MATH: 9,\quad 5,\quad 12,\quad 4,\quad 16]

Content:
What is the third order statistic [MATH: x_{(3)}] for this sample?

Content:
[MATH: x_{(1)} = 4,\quad x_{(2)} = 5,\quad x_{(3)} = 9,\quad x_{(4)} = 12,\quad x_{(5)} = 16]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Given an I.I.D random sample from a probability distribution, suppose we needed to know the probability that the third largest value was less than [MATH: 10,] or the probability that the second smallest value was greater than [MATH: 5.]

Content:
To find such probabilities, we first need to put the values in the sample in ascending order. This is where we use so-called order statistics.

Content:
For an I.I.D random sample [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots X_n,] the order statistics are obtained by arranging the values in ascending order. The [MATH: r]th order statistic, denoted [MATH: X_{(r)},] is the [MATH: r]th smallest value in the ordered sample. Specifically,

Content:
- the first order statistic is [MATH: X_{(1)} = \min\left\{X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots, X_n\right\},]
- the second order statistic is [MATH: X_{(2)} =] the second smallest of [MATH: \left\{X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots, X_n\right\},]
- the third order statistic: [MATH: X_{(3)} =] the third smallest of [MATH: \left\{X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots, X_n\right\},]
- [MATH: \vdots]
- the [MATH: r]th order statistic is [MATH: X_{(r)} =] the [MATH: r]th smallest of [MATH: \left\{X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots, X_n\right\},]
- [MATH: \vdots]
- the [MATH: n]th order statistic is [MATH: X_{(n)} = \max\left\{X_1, X_2, X_3, \ldots, X_n\right\}.]

Content:
To demonstrate, consider the following sample taken from the I.I.D random sample [MATH: X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_5.]

Content:
[MATH: 9,\quad 5,\quad 12,\quad 4,\quad 16]

Content:
What is the third order statistic [MATH: x_{(3)}] for this sample?

Content:
To find the third order statistic for this sample, we first sort the numbers in increasing order:

Content:
[MATH: x_{(1)} = 4,\quad x_{(2)} = 5,\quad x_{(3)} = 9,\quad x_{(4)} = 12,\quad x_{(5)} = 16]

Content:
Therefore, the third order statistic for this sample is [MATH: x_{(3)} = 9.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Calculating Probabilities Associated With Maximums

Content:
[MATH: X_{(1)} < X_{(2)} < X_{(3)} < \cdots < X_{(n)}]

Content:
We wish to find [MATH: P\left(X_{(3)} < 2\right).] This can only happen if all [MATH: X_i]'s in our sample are smaller than [MATH: 2.] One such configuration is shown below.

[MATH: P(X_{(1)} > 0)|= P(X_{1} > 0, X_{2} > 0, X_{3} > 0); = P(X_{1} > 0) ⋅ P(X_{2} > 0) ⋅ P(X_{3} > 0).]

Each [MATH: X_i \sim N(1,2^2),] so, we transform [MATH: X] into a standard normal random variable [MATH: Z] by [MATH: z]-scoring:
[MATH: P(X_{i} > 0)|= P(Z > (0 − 1)/(2)); = P(Z > − 0.5)]
